Perceptions and Reported Support for Political Violence

In Study 1 (N = 408; US participants; pre-registered), as hypothesized, we find that although support for political violence is rare and overestimated among both parties, Democrats' outgroup perceptions were significantly more pessimistic than Republicans' (d = 0.34 for murder; d = 0.36 for assault; d = 0.39 for arson; all ps < .001) (see Figs. 1 and 2). Across our three measures of political violence (i.e., murder, assault, and arson), Democrats, on average, predict that 29.60% of Republicans will report supporting political violence. This exceeds the actual share of Republicans who report supporting political violence (1.83% averaged across our three measures) by 1,517%. In contrast, Republicans predict that 19.48% of Democrats report supporting political violence. This exceeds the actual share of Democrats who report supporting political violence (3.54%) by 450%.

These patterns emerge consistently across arson, assault with a deadly weapon, and murder, as Democrats' outgroup perceptions are approximately 10 percentage points higher than Republicans' outgroup perceptions on all three types of violence (see Fig. 1). Democrats, on average, predict that 33.90% of Republicans will report supporting arson, that 29.42% of Republicans will report supporting assault with a deadly weapon, and that 25.49% of Republicans will report supporting murder. In contrast, Republicans predict that 22.87% of Democrats will report supporting arson, that 19.51% of Democrats will report supporting assault with a deadly weapon, and that 16.05% of Democrats will report supporting murder. Conversely, we do not find evidence that Democrats' average ingroup perceptions differ from Republicans' (p = .35). Across our three measures of political violence, Democrats, on average, predict that 13.42% of other Democrats support political violence, while Republicans predict that 11.67% of other Republicans support political violence. More specifically, Democrats, on average, predict that 17.81% of other Democrats will report supporting arson, that 12.45% of other Democrats will report supporting assault with a deadly weapon, and that 10.01% of other Democrats will report supporting murder. Similarly, Republicans predict that 13.43% of other Republicans will report supporting arson, that 11.84% of other Republicans will report supporting assault with a deadly weapon, and that 9.76% of other Republicans will report supporting murder.

We also do not find evidence that actual reported support for political violence differs between Democrats and Republicans (all ps > .08). More specifically, 5.80% of Democrats report supporting arson compared to 1.99% of Republicans; 1.93% of Democrats report supporting assault with a deadly weapon compared to 2.49% of Republicans; and 2.90% of Democrats report supporting murder compared to 1.00% of Republicans.

Collectively, this suggests that the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry is unique to intergroup perceptions rather than reflecting a broader difference in beliefs about how widespread political violence support is among most Americans or an underlying difference in actual reported political violence support.

Meta-Perceptions of Support for Political Violence

To further explore asymmetries in perceived support for political violence, we examined Democrats' and Republicans' meta-perceptions (i.e., how one believes their group is perceived by others). Our consideration of meta-perceptions is informed by previous findings that inaccurate meta-perceptions can contribute to polarization (36https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/hc12y+6HGuV 37) https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/hx9Za dehumanization (38) , and support for undemocratic practices (39). Given the observed asymmetry in perceptions of outgroup support for political violence, we expect Democrats to also hold more negative meta-perceptions than Republicans. Indeed, we find evidence that Democrats' beliefs about what Republicans believe about them are too pessimistic (d = 0.56 for murder; d = 0.55 for assault; d = 0.61 for arson; all ps < .001). Democrats, on average, predicted Republicans would estimate that 35.25% of Democrats support political violence, nearly twice Republicans' actual prediction (19.48%). By contrast, there are no significant differences between Republicans' metaperceptions and Democrats' actual outgroup perceptions (all ps > .16) (see Fig. S1). Republicans, on average, predicted Democrats would estimate that 26.19% of Republicans support political violence, close to Democrats' actual prediction (29.60%). This asymmetry is partially due to Democrats' meta-perceptions reflecting greater pessimism in absolute terms, not just relative to actual outgroup perceptions (d = 0.33 for murder; d = 0.29 for assault; d = 0.36 for arson; all ps < .005). These patterns are consistent across arson, assault, and murder (see SI and Fig. S1 for details). This suggests that-at least within the domain of political violence-Democrats hold more pessimistic views about how Republicans view Democrats than vice versa, potentially contributing to the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry in predicted outgroup support for political violence.

Concern About Politically Violent Extremists

To the extent that Democrats expect a higher share of Republicans to support political violence, Democrats may also be more concerned about politically violent outgroup extremists. We investigate this possibility by measuring participants' levels of concern about ingroup and outgroup extremists (defined as those who support political violence) as threats to public safety, future election security, US democracy, and America. We also assess concern via perceived importance of protecting against ingroup and outgroup extremists. Finally, we examine the actual and perceived share of Democrats and Republicans who report concern about the possibility of a civil war occurring in the US.

We find that both Republicans and Democrats are more concerned about outgroup than ingroup extremists as threats to all four outcomes (all ps < .001 based on paired t-tests; see SI and Fig. S2 for details). Yet, again, we find that Democrats are more concerned than Republicans about outgroup extremists as threats to public safety (M = 7.09, SD = 2.05 for Democrats; M = 6.63, SD = 2.45 for Republicans; d = 0.21, t(389) = 2.07, p = .039), future election security (M = 7.49, SD = 1.91 for Democrats; M = 6.83, SD = 2.39 for Republicans; d = 0.31, t(382) = 3.11, p = .002), US democracy (M = 7.55, SD = 1.84 for Democrats; M = 6.72, SD = 2.40 for Republicans; d = 0.39, t(375) = 3.90, p < .001), and America (M = 7.50, SD = 1.83 for Democrats; M = 6.85, SD = 2.43 for Republicans; d = 0.31, t(371) = 3.08, p = .002). In contrast, we do not observe significant differences between Democrats' and Republicans' concerns about ingroup extremists (all ps > .13).

We observe a similar Democrat-Republican asymmetry in the perceived importance of protecting against outgroup extremists (see Fig. 2). Democrats rate protecting against outgroup extremists (M = 7.90, SD = 1.72) as significantly more important than Republicans do (M = 7.33, SD = 2.27; d = 0.29, t(373) = 2.88, p = .004). As expected, this asymmetry does not emerge for protecting against ingroup extremists (M = 6.81, SD = 2.47 for Democrats; M = 7.04, SD = 2.44 for Republicans; t(406) = 0.96, p = .34). Furthermore, only Democrats view protecting against outgroup extremists as significantly more important than protecting against ingroup extremists (t(206) = 6.77, p < .001).

Consistent with our previous findings, a greater share of Democrats (60.87%) expressed civil war concern than Republicans (49.75%) (𝛸𝛸 2 (1, N = 408) = 4.66, p = .031). Furthermore, in contrast to perceptions of extremists, both Democrats and Republicans significantly underestimated the share of ingroup and outgroup members who are concerned about a potential civil war (all ps < .001; see SI and Fig. S3 for details). We also do not observe Democrat-Republican asymmetries in outgroup perceptions of civil war concern (M = 42.23, SD = 25.07 for Democrats; M = 40.57, SD = 25.07 for Republicans; t(406) = 0.67, p = .50), suggesting that the prior asymmetries do not simply reflect broad differences in intergroup perceptions but are instead specific to political violence.

Study 2

In Study 2, we replicated our main results from Study 1 using a large sample that was nationally representative with respect to sex, age, and ethnicity (N = 906; US participants; pre-registered). Given the consistency of responses across all three measures in Study 1, in Study 2, we measured support for political violence using only the murder vignette while omitting arson and deadly assault (see Methods for details).

We also included several additional measures to explore the boundaries of the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry. Specifically, we measured ingroup, outgroup, and meta-perceptions of affect. We assessed the perceived prevalence of support for political violence among the most extreme ingroup and outgroup supporters, as well as among ingroup and outgroup leaders. Additionally, we assessed participants' perceptions of whether typical outgroup members are more aggressive than typical ingroup members.

As a control measure, we examined reported and perceived support for drug trafficking, a non-politically-motivated crime. We also included an alternative measure of levels of support for political violence used in previous studies (4, 16) and randomized whether participants saw this alternative measure before or after the vignette-based measures. Finally, we randomly assigned half of our participants to receive financial incentives for accuracy (40).

Perceptions and Reported Support for Political Violence

Replicating the main results of Study 1, we find that Democrats' outgroup perceptions of support for political violence are significantly more pessimistic than Republicans' (d = 0.23, p < .001), although both parties overestimate and rarely report support for political violence (see Figs. 3 and 4). On average, Democrats predict that 22.57% of Republicans report supporting politically-motivated murder. This exceeds the actual share of Republicans who report supporting politically-motivated murder (0.97%) by 2,227%. Republicans on average predict that 16.90% of Democrats report supporting politicallymotivated murder. This exceeds the actual share of Democrats who report supporting politically-motivated murder (1.42%) by 1,090%.

Again, we find no evidence that Democrats' ingroup perceptions of political violence support differ from Republicans' (d = 0.06, p = .36). Democrats, on average, predict that 10.10% of other Democrats support political violence, while Republicans predict that 9.05% of other Republicans support political violence. We also do not find evidence that reported support for political violence differs between Democrats and Republicans (𝛸𝛸 2 (1, N = 906) = 0.09, p = .760).

In Study 2, we complemented our vignette-based measure of support for political violence with an alternative, more abstract measure used in previous research (4, 16, 35, 41). This alternative measure asks participants to rate their level of support for political violence using a 0-100 scale, rather than providing discrete choices. Our findings suggest that the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry appears consistently across both measures. In contrast to prior work, we find Democrats are more pessimistic than Republicans about outgroup members, regardless of whether they responded to this abstract, alternative measure before (d = 0.44, p < .001) or after (d = 0.27, p = .004) the vignette-based measures. This suggests that the Democrat-Republican asymmetry can emerge even in the absence of a defined context for violence and provides evidence that Democrats may have relatively recently adopted a view of outgroup members as politically violent, regardless of how political violence is defined.

Meta-Perceptions of Support for Political Violence

As in Study 1, we find evidence of a Democrat-Republican asymmetry in metaperceptions of politically-motivated violence support. Democrats' beliefs about Republicans' outgroup perceptions are again too pessimistic (d = 0.57, p < .001). In contrast, we find only a marginal difference between Republicans' meta-perceptions and Democrats' outgroup perceptions (d = 0.13, p = .059) (see Fig. 4 and SI). As in Study 1, we again find that this asymmetry is partially due to Democrats' meta-perceptions reflecting greater pessimism in absolute terms, not just relative to actual outgroup perceptions (d = 0.20, p = .003). Democrats, on average, predicted Republicans would estimate that 31.01% of Democrats report supporting political violence, nearly twice Republicans' actual prediction (16.90%). Republicans, on average, predicted Democrats would estimate that 25.78% of Republicans would report supporting political violence, slightly higher than Democrats' actual prediction (22.57%).

Concern About Politically Violent Extremists

Replicating the results of Study 1, we find that Democrats are more concerned than Republicans about outparty extremists as threats to future election security (M = 7.53, SD = 1.98 for Democrats; M = 6.99, SD = 2.21 for Republicans; d = 0.26, t(833) = 3.86, p < .001), US democracy (M = 7.47, SD = 2.02 for Democrats; M = 6.92, SD = 2.32 for Republicans; d = 0.25, t(821) = 3.76, p < .001), and America (M = 7.36, SD = 2.02 for Democrats; M = 6.97, SD = 2.30 for Republicans; d = 0.18, t(824) = 2.65, p = .008). However, here Democrats are only marginally more concerned than Republicans about outgroup extremists as threats to public safety (M = 7.11, SD = 2.18 for Democrats; M = 6.85, SD = 2.38 for Republicans; d = 0.11, t(842) = 1.70, p = .090). We again do not observe significant differences between Democrats' and Republicans' concern about ingroup extremists (all ps > .56). We also find that Republicans and Democrats are both more concerned about outgroup than ingroup extremists as threats to all four outcomes (all ps < .001 based on paired t-tests; see SI and Fig. S4 for details).

In contrast to Study 1, both Democrats and Republicans view protecting against outgroup extremists (M = 8.02, SD = 1.71 for Democrats; M = 7.60, SD = 2.07 for Republicans) as significantly more important than protecting against ingroup extremists (M = 7.17, SD = 2.52 for Democrats; M = 7.13, SD = 2.47 for Republicans; both ps < .001). However, we again find that Democrats view protecting against outgroup extremists as significantly more important than Republicans (p = .001).

In Study 2, we also find that a majority of Democrats (53.04%) and Republicans (57.04%) report concern about the possibility of a civil war occurring in the US. Replicating the results of Study 1, we do not observe Democrat-Republican asymmetries in the perceived share of outgroup or ingroup members who report concern about a potential civil war (both ps > .16). Both Democrats and Republicans also significantly underestimated the share of ingroup and outgroup members who report concern about a potential civil war (all ps < .001; see SI and Fig. S5).

Boundaries of Democrat-Republican Asymmetry

Why might Democrats show greater pessimism than Republicans about outparty support for political violence, and what is the scope of Democrat-Republican asymmetries? We examine several related asymmetries to clarify the boundaries of this pattern.

Negative Outgroup Affect and Meta-Perceptions.

First, we explore whether similar asymmetries exist for outparty affect (39, 42, 43). We find that, relative to Republicans, Democrats report more negative outgroup affect (M = 22.64, SD = 20.71 for Democrats; M = 32.47, SD = 25.12 for Republicans; d = -0.43, t(796) = -6.35, p < .001) and metaperceptions of affect (M = 18.43, SD = 17.76 for Democrats; M = 21.83, SD = 19.18 for Republicans; t(848) = -2.75, p = .006). By contrast, Democrats do not feel more negative towards their ingroup than Republicans do (p = .462).

Views of Most Extreme Outgroup Members.

Second, we assess whether Democrats are more pessimistic than Republicans about the most extreme outgroup members' support for political violence, as these views could generalize to the outgroup or lead to extreme perceptions of the outgroup's behavioral norms (44). Consistent with this explanation, when asked to imagine a group of the most extreme outgroup members, Democrats were significantly more pessimistic than Republicans about the share of extreme outgroup members who support political violence (M = 60.59, SD = 31.84 for Democrats; M = 46.74, SD = 35.00 for Republicans; d = 0.42, t(840) = 6.18, p < .001). That is, Democrats believed, on average, that 60.59% of the most extreme Republicans support political violence, whereas Republicans believed, on average, that 46.74% of the most extreme Democrats support political violence. However, there was no such asymmetry for the most extreme ingroup members (p = .138).

Perceived Aggressiveness of Outgroup. Third, Democrats may view Republicans as especially violent or aggressive in general, not just in political contexts. To assess this possibility, we compare levels of agreement with the statement that the typical outgroup member is more aggressive than the typical ingroup member. We find that Democrats endorse this statement significantly more than Republicans (M = 7.05, SD = 1.71 for Democrats; M = 6.05, SD = 2.30 for Republicans; d = 0.50, t(746) = 7.30, p < .001), suggesting that Democrats may perceive Republicans as more aggressive overall.

Perceptions and Reported Support for Non-Political Crime. Fourth, Democrats may view Republicans as more supportive of crime generally. We find that while support for non-political crime (i.e., drug trafficking) is also rare and overestimated, we do not observe a significant asymmetry between Democrats' and Republicans' outgroup predictions (M = 9.90, SD = 20.61 for Democrats; M = 12.31, SD = 20.53 for Republicans; d = -0.12, t(876) = -1.76, p = .080). We also find evidence that the difference in Democrats' and Republicans' outgroup predictions is larger for politicallymotivated murder than for non-political crime, as there is a significant interaction between non-political crime and Republican party identification (d = -0.21, p < .001; see SI for details). As expected, we do not find evidence of a Democrat-Republican asymmetry for ingroup predictions of drug trafficking support (d = 0.02, p = .796) (see Fig. 3). These results-in combination with the observed asymmetry in outgroup aggressiveness-suggest that Democrats may perceive Republicans as specifically more violent (and thus supportive of political violence), rather than reflecting a generalized pessimism about Republicans' support for criminal behavior.

Views of Outgroup Leaders. Fifth, we explore whether Democrats perceive more widespread support for political violence among outgroup leaders than Republicans. That is, Democrats may view Republican leaders (e.g., Donald Trump) as more combative or supportive of violence than Republicans view Democrat leaders (e.g., Joe Biden and Kamala Harris). This may negatively bias Democrats' perceptions and meta-perceptions while moderating Republicans'. Yet, we find no significant asymmetry between Democrats' and Republicans' perceptions of outparty leaders' political violence support (M = 21.01, SD = 24.29 for Democrats; M = 18.39, SD = 26.95 for Republicans; d = 0.10, t(837) = 1.52, p = .128), suggesting that the observed asymmetries are not driven by generalized views about outparty politicians who use violent rhetoric or subvert democratic norms. Notably, we also find that Republicans' perceptions of ingroup leaders are more negative than Democrats' (M = 6.65, SD = 14.02 for Democrats; M = 9.70, SD = 18.95 for Republicans; d = -0.19, t(743) = -2.71, p = .007).

Financial Incentives for Accuracy.

Sixth, Democrats may exaggerate their stated outgroup perceptions to signal their political identity (45). However, we find that providing financial incentives for accuracy has no significant effect on outgroup predictions among Democrats (d = 0.11, p = .223) or Republicans (d = -0.11, p = .267). This suggests that respondents are reporting sincerely held beliefs rather than intentionally inflating their predictions to align with their political identity.

Together, these results help rule out expressive responding as an explanation for Democrats' heightened pessimism. They also suggest that Democrats are not significantly more pessimistic about Republicans' support for all crime than vice versa, and we do not find evidence that Democrats are generalizing from their perceptions of outparty leaders. Rather, the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry may reflect generalizations from Democrats' views of extreme outgroup members and/or their overall views of Republicans as aggressive.

Study 3

In Study 3 (N = 1,505; US participants; pre-registered), we replicated our main results from Studies 1 and 2 and tested whether exposure to a fictional violent or non-violent outparty exemplar causally impacts partisan misperceptions and meta-perceptions of political violence support (see Methods for details). As in Study 2, our sample was nationally representative with respect to sex, age, and ethnicity. In Study 3, we also examined whether any exemplar effects are mediated by availability-based processes, namely heightened cognitive accessibility of violent outparty members. We additionally assessed associative and stereotype-based pathways, including strengthened outpartyviolence associations and increased beliefs about outparty aggressiveness, as potential mediators.

Perceptions and Reported Support for Political Violence

Replicating the main results of Studies 1 and 2, we find that Democrats' outgroup perceptions of support for political violence are significantly more pessimistic than Republicans' (d = 0.20, p < .001), although both parties overestimate outparty political violence support and themselves rarely report supporting political violence (see Figs. 5 and 6). On average, Democrats predict that 25.01% of Republicans report supporting politically-motivated murder. This exceeds the actual share of Republicans who report supporting politically-motivated murder (1.06%) by 2,259%. Republicans on average predict that 19.92% of Democrats report supporting politically-motivated murder. This exceeds the actual share of Democrats who report supporting politically-motivated murder (1.33%) by 1,398%.

Again, we find no evidence that Democrats' ingroup perceptions of political violence support differ from Republicans' (d = 0.02, p = .66). Democrats, on average, predict that 10.55% of other Democrats support political violence, while Republicans predict that 10.17% of other Republicans support political violence. We also do not find evidence that reported support for political violence differs between Democrats and Republicans (𝛸𝛸 2 (1, N = 1,505) = 0.05, p = .815).

We next tested whether exposure to a violent or non-violent outparty exemplar affected perceptions of outgroup political violence support. Overall, we find exposure to a violent exemplar increased perceived outparty support for political violence relative to a null control (b = 5.68, SE = 1.57, t(1499) = 3.61, p < .001, d = 0.23). In contrast, exposure to a non-violent exemplar did not affect perceived outparty support relative to control (b = 1.71, SE = 1.58, t(1499) = 1.09, p = .523, d = 0.07). Overall, participants in the violentexemplar condition estimated that 25.7% of outparty members report supporting politically motivated murder (vs. 20.0% in control; 21.7% in the non-violent condition).

There was no significant Condition × Party interaction (ps > .687), but simple-effects analyses indicated that the violent-exemplar effect was significant among Democrats (b = 6.31, SE = 2.23, t(1499) = 2.84, p = .013, d = 0.24) and not significant among Republicans (b = 5.05, SE = 2.23, t(1499) = 2.26, p = .061, d = 0.21).

Comparing across conditions, we find that exposure to a violent outparty exemplar brought Republicans' estimates in line with Democrats' baseline perceptions. Democrats in the control condition predicted that 22.25% of Republicans support politically motivated murder. Republicans exposed to a violent outparty exemplar predicted that 22.81% of Democrats support politically motivated murder (b = -0.56, SE = 2.23, t(1499) = -0.25, p = .801). This pattern suggests that previously observed Democrat-Republican asymmetries in perceived outparty violence support may partly reflect differential availability of extreme outparty exemplars, rather than stable partisan differences in pessimism. Notably, however, Democrats exposed to a violent exemplar further increased their estimates of outparty members' support for political violence, underscoring that exemplar-driven salience can amplify pessimism across both parties.

What psychological processes underlie the effect of violent exemplars on perceptions of outgroup support for political violence? We tested three preregistered mechanisms: (1) heightened cognitive availability of violent outparty members, (2) stronger associative links between the outparty and violence, and (3) generalized beliefs about outparty aggressiveness. As preregistered, we first estimated separate single-mediator models to test whether each pathway independently accounted for exemplar effects.

We find a significant indirect effect of cognitive availability of violent outparty members on partisans' perceptions of outgroup support for political violence (ACME = 0.06, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10], p = .007). We also find a significant direct effect (ADE = 0.17, 95% CI [0.05, 0.28], p = .003) and total effect (0.23, 95% CI [0.10, 0.35], p < .001). The indirect effect mediated approximately 26.4% of the total effect.

We also find a significant indirect effect of generalized beliefs about outparty aggressiveness on partisans' perceptions of outgroup support for political violence (ACME = 0.05, 95% CI [0.01, 0.09], p = .018). We also find a significant direct effect (ADE = 0.18, 95% CI [0.06, 0.29], p = .005) and total effect (0.22, 95% CI [0.04, 0.50], p = .019). The indirect effect mediated approximately 21.6% of the total effect. By contrast, although there was a directionally similar effect of associative strength between violence and the outparty, the indirect effect did not reach statistical significance (ACME = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.00, 0.11], p = .055). There was a significant direct effect (ADE = 0.17, 95% CI [0.06, 0.28], p = .002) and total effect (0.23, 95% CI [0.10, 0.35], p < .001).

As pre-registered, we then fit a serial mediation model to assess whether violent exemplars increased accessibility of violent outparty representations, which in turn heightened perceived outparty aggressiveness and increased perceived outparty violence support. We find evidence consistent with a significant indirect pathway (0.04, 95% CI [0.01, 0.07], z = 2.78, p = .005), suggesting that exposure to a violent outparty exemplar increases perceptions of outgroup violence support, in part, by elevating the cognitive accessibility of violent exemplars and, subsequently, perceived outparty aggressiveness.

These results are consistent with patterns observed within the control condition, as Democrats (relative to Republicans) reported more pessimistic perceptions of outgroup political violence support (d = 0.19, p = .033), higher cognitive availability of violent outparty members (d = 0.48, p < .001), beliefs that outparty members were more aggressive (d = 0.48, p < .001), and greater associative strength between violence and the outparty (d = 0.41, p < .001).

Meta-Perceptions of Support for Political Violence

As in Studies 1 and 2, we find evidence of a Democrat-Republican asymmetry in metaperceptions of politically-motivated violence support. Democrats' beliefs about Republicans' outgroup perceptions are again too pessimistic (d = 0.59, p < .001). In contrast, we find no significant difference between Republicans' meta-perceptions and Democrats' outgroup perceptions (d = 0.01, p = .785) (see Fig. 6 and SI). As in Studies 1 and 2, we again find that this asymmetry is partially due to Democrats' meta-perceptions reflecting greater pessimism in absolute terms, not just relative to actual outgroup perceptions (d = 0.37, p < .001). Democrats, on average, predicted Republicans would estimate that 34.98% of Democrats report supporting political violence, significantly higher than Republicans' actual prediction (19.92%). Republicans, on average, predicted Democrats would estimate that 25.37% of Republicans would report supporting political violence, close to Democrats' actual prediction (25.01%).

We next tested whether exposure to a violent or non-violent outparty exemplar affected meta-perceptions of political violence support. We find no evidence that either violent or non-violent exemplars shifted meta-perceptions relative to the control condition (violent vs. control: b = 2.57, SE = 1.65, t(1499) = 1.56, p = .263; non-violent vs. control: b = 0.32, SE = 1.65, t(1499) = 0.20, p = .979). These effects did not differ by party (all Condition × Party ps > .980). Thus, whereas violent exemplars increased perceptions of outparty violence support, they did not meaningfully shift beliefs about how one's own group is viewed by the outparty.

Boundaries of Democrat-Republican Asymmetry

In Study 3, we replicate several of the additional Democrat-Republican asymmetries found in Study 2.

More specifically, we again find that relative to Republicans, Democrats report more negative outgroup affect (M = 19.92, SD = 21.89 for Democrats; M = 36.39, SD = 24.70 for Republicans; d = -0.71, t(1481) = -13.69, p < .001) and meta-perceptions of affect (M = 19.21, SD = 17.97 for Democrats; M = 26.14, SD = 21.04 for Republicans; d = -0.35, t(1467) = -6.87, p < .001). By contrast, Democrats do not feel more negative towards their ingroup than Republicans do (p = .105).

As in Study 2, we find Democrats were significantly more pessimistic than Republicans about the share of extreme outgroup members who support political violence (M = 56.72, SD = 33.34 for Democrats; M = 41.99, SD = 33.18 for Republicans; d = 0.44, t(1503) = 8.59, p < .001). That is, Democrats believed, on average, that 56.72% of the most extreme Republicans support political violence, whereas Republicans believed, on average, that 41.99% of the most extreme Democrats support political violence. However, there was only a marginal asymmetry for the most extreme ingroup members (p = .070).

Replicating Study 2, we do not find a significant asymmetry between Democrats' and Republicans' outgroup predictions of support for non-political crime (i.e., drug trafficking) (M = 12.24, SD = 22.71 for Democrats; M = 13.54, SD = 20.39 for Republicans; d = -0.06, t(1486) = -1.18, p = .240). We also find evidence that the difference in Democrats' and Republicans' outgroup predictions is larger for politicallymotivated murder than for non-political crime, as there is a significant interaction between non-political crime and Republican party identification (d = -0.29, p < .001; see SI for details). As expected, we do not find evidence of a Democrat-Republican asymmetry for ingroup predictions of drug trafficking support (d = 0.02, p = .718) (see Fig. 5).

In contrast to Study 2, in Study 3 we find Democrats are significantly more pessimistic than Republicans about outparty leaders' political violence support (M = 25.32, SD = 29.71 for Democrats; M = 16.44, SD = 23.34 for Republicans; d = 0.33, t(1424) = 6.45, p < .001). Conversely, we find that Republicans' perceptions of ingroup leaders are more negative than Democrats' (M = 6.58, SD = 15.38 for Democrats; M = 8.26, SD = 16.66 for Republicans; d = -0.10, t(1493) = -2.03, p = .043).

In Study 3, we also find that a majority of Democrats (58.96%) and many Republicans (42.82%) report concern about the possibility of a civil war occurring in the US.

Study 4

In Study 4 (N = 620; Indian participants; pre-registered), we examined whether the main results from Studies 1-3 can generalize beyond the United States by testing for a similar asymmetry between supporters of India's two major political alliances: the N.D.A. alliance and the I.N.D.I.A. alliance. As expected, I.N.D.I.A. supporters identified as significantly more left ideologically than N.D.A. supporters on a 0 (left) to 10 (right) scale (M = 5.02 vs. M = 7.11; t(602) = -8.97, p < .001). As in Studies 2 and 3, we measured support for political violence using the murder vignette and support for nonpolitical crime using the drug trafficking vignette. We additionally measured affect, perceptions of outgroup and ingroup leaders' support for violence, and perceptions of the most extreme outgroup and ingroup members' support for violence (see Methods for details).

Perceptions and Reported Support for Political Violence

Replicating the main results of Studies 1-3, we find that I.N.D.I.A. supporters' outgroup perceptions of support for political violence are significantly more pessimistic than N.D.A. supporters' (d = 0.18, 95% CI [0.02, 0.33], t(616) = 2.20, p = .028), although both groups overestimate outgroup support for political violence (see Figs. 7 and 8). On average, I.N.D.I.A. supporters predict that 38.04% of N.D.A. supporters report supporting politically-motivated murder. This exceeds the actual share of N.D.A. supporters who report supporting politically-motivated murder (16.61%) by 129%. N.D.A. supporters on average predict that 32.45% of I.N.D.I.A. supporters report supporting politically-motivated murder. This exceeds the actual share of I.N.D.I.A. supporters who report supporting politically-motivated murder (15.99%) by 103%. Conversely, we do not find evidence that I.N.D.I.A. supporters' ingroup perceptions of political violence support differ from N.D.A. supporters' (d = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.23], t(613) = 0.87, p = .382). I.N.D.I.A. supporters, on average, predict that 34.07% of other I.N.D.I.A. supporters support politically-motivated murder, while N.D.A. supporters predict that 31.77% of other N.D.A. supporters support politically-motivated murder. We also do not find evidence that actual reported support for political violence differs between I.N.D.I.A. and N.D.A. supporters (15.99% vs. 16.61%; 𝛸𝛸 2 (1, N = 620) = 0.01, p = .919).

As expected, I.N.D.I.A. supporters were significantly more pessimistic about outgroup members' support for political violence than about ingroup members' support (mean difference = 3.97, t(318) = 2.27, p = .024). However, N.D.A. supporters' outgroup and ingroup predictions did not significantly differ (mean difference = 0.68, t(300) = 0.37, p = .708).

Meta-Perceptions of Support for Political Violence

As in Studies 1-3, we find evidence of an asymmetry in meta-perceptions of politicallymotivated violence support. I.N.D.I.A. supporters' beliefs about N.D.A. supporters' outgroup perceptions are again too pessimistic (d = 0.37, t(599) = 4.53, p < .001). In contrast, we find no significant difference between N.D.A. supporters' meta-perceptions and I.N.D.I.A. supporters' actual outgroup perceptions (d = -0.09, t(618) = -1.10, p = .273) (see Fig. 8). As in Studies 1-3, we again find that this asymmetry is partially due to I.N.D.I.A. supporters' meta-perceptions reflecting greater pessimism in absolute terms, not just relative to actual outgroup perceptions (d = 0.28, t(613) = 3.49, p < .001). I.N.D.I.A. supporters, on average, predicted N.D.A. supporters would estimate that 43.37% of I.N.D.I.A. supporters report supporting political violence, significantly higher than N.D.A. supporters' actual prediction (32.45%). N.D.A. supporters, on average, predicted I.N.D.I.A. supporters would estimate that 35.37% of N.D.A. supporters report supporting political violence, close to I.N.D.I.A. supporters' actual prediction (38.04%).

Concern About Politically Violent Extremists

In contrast to Studies 1 and 2, we find little evidence that I.N.D.I.A. supporters are more concerned than N.D.A. supporters about outgroup extremists. I.N.D.I.A. supporters were more concerned about outgroup extremists as threats to India's democracy (M = 6.62, SD = 2.47 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 6.16, SD = 2.59 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.18, t(611) = 2.26, p = .024). However, the two groups did not differ in their concern about outgroup extremists as threats to public safety (M = 6.42, SD = 2.41 vs. M = 6.28, SD = 2.35; d = 0.06, t(617) = 0.72, p = .471), future election security (M = 6.45, SD = 2.35 vs. M = 6.22, SD = 2.44; d = 0.10, t(612) = 1.22, p = .222), or India (M = 6.24, SD = 2.63 vs. M = 6.28, SD = 2.66; d = -0.02, t(615) = -0.19, p = .847). As in Studies 1 and 2, we do not observe significant differences between I.N.D.I.A. and N.D.A. supporters' concern about ingroup extremists (all ps > .35). We also find that both I.N.D.I.A. and N.D.A. supporters are more concerned about outgroup than ingroup extremists as threats to all four outcomes (all ps < .001 based on paired t-tests; see SI).

We also do not observe an I.N.D.I.A.-N.D.A. asymmetry in the perceived importance of protecting against outgroup extremists (M = 6.65, SD = 2.41 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 6.46, SD = 2.45 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.08, t(615) = 0.97, p = .330) or ingroup extremists (M = 6.14, SD = 2.46 vs. M = 6.01, SD = 2.69; d = 0.05, t(605) = 0.63, p = .527). As in Study 2, both I.N.D.I.A. supporters (t(318) = 3.47, p < .001) and N.D.A. supporters (t(300) = 2.71, p = .007) view protecting against outgroup extremists as significantly more important than protecting against ingroup extremists.

Consistent with Study 1, a greater share of I.N.D.I.A. supporters (75.86%) than N.D.A. supporters (60.13%) expressed concern about the possibility of a civil war occurring in India, (𝛸𝛸² (1, N = 620) = 16.96, p < .001). As in Studies 1 and 2, we do not observe an I.N.D.I.A.-N.D.A. asymmetry in outgroup perceptions of civil war concern (M = 44.68, SD = 27.52 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 42.88, SD = 29.48 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.06, t(608) = 0.79, p = .432). In contrast to Study 2, however, I.N.D.I.A. supporters estimated that a larger share of their ingroup is concerned about a civil war than N.D.A. supporters did (M = 49.20, SD = 28.02 vs. M = 41.90, SD = 30.84; d = 0.25, t(604) = 3.08, p = .002).

Boundaries of I.N.D.I.A.-N.D.A. Asymmetry

In Study 4, we replicate several of the additional asymmetries found in Studies 2 and 3.

As in Study 3, I.N.D.I.A. supporters were significantly more pessimistic than N.D.A. supporters about outparty leaders' political violence support (M = 44.47, SD = 33.10 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 37.70, SD = 32.34 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.21, t(617) = 2.58, p = .010). We do not find evidence of an asymmetry in perceptions of ingroup leaders (M = 35.39, SD = 30.95 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 33.66, SD = 31.61 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.06, t(614) = 0.69, p = .490).

As in Studies 2 and 3, I.N.D.I.A. supporters were also significantly more pessimistic than N.D.A. supporters about the share of extreme outgroup members who support political violence (M = 53.74, SD = 33.48 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 45.35, SD = 34.03 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.25, t(615) = 3.09, p = .002). That is, I.N.D.I.A. supporters believed, on average, that 53.74% of the most extreme N.D.A. supporters support political violence, whereas N.D.A. supporters believed, on average, that 45.35% of the most extreme I.N.D.I.A. supporters support political violence. However, there was no such asymmetry for the most extreme ingroup members (M = 43.77, SD = 31.51 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 42.44, SD = 33.91 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.04, t(608) = 0.50, p = .615).

As in Studies 2 and 3, we do not find a significant asymmetry between I.N.D.I.A. and N.D.A. supporters' outgroup predictions of support for non-political crime (i.e., drug trafficking) (M = 30.86, SD = 31.81 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 28.05, SD = 32.69 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.09, t(614) = 1.08, p = .279), nor for ingroup predictions of drug trafficking support (M = 26.37 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 27.20 for N.D.A. supporters; d = -0.03, t(608) = -0.33, p = .743). Both groups significantly overestimated drug trafficking support among ingroup and outgroup members relative to actual reported support (7.21% among I.N.D.I.A. supporters; 6.98% among N.D.A. supporters; all ps < .001) (see Fig. 7). In contrast to Studies 2 and 3, however, we do not find evidence that the difference between I.N.D.I.A. and N.D.A. supporters' outgroup predictions is larger for politically-motivated murder than for non-political crime, as the interaction between crime type and alliance was not significant (b = 2.77, SE = 3.63, t(1236) = 0.77, p = .445). Interestingly, although outgroup and ingroup predictions of drug trafficking support did not differ, I.N.D.I.A. supporters held more pessimistic meta-perceptions of drug trafficking support than N.D.A. supporters did (M = 36.56 vs. M = 31.60; t(615) = 2.08, p = .038).

Unlike in Studies 2 and 3, here we do not find that I.N.D.I.A. supporters report more negative outgroup affect than N.D.A. supporters (M = 46.13 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 44.39 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.06, t(607) = 0.75, p = .456) or more negative metaperceptions of affect (M = 44.12 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 42.60 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.05, t(608) = 0.65, p = .515). I.N.D.I.A. supporters also do not feel more negative towards their ingroup than N.D.A. supporters do (M = 69.51 vs. M = 69.69; t(607) = -0.10, p = .924). Unlike in Studies 2 and 3, we also do not find that I.N.D.I.A. supporters view the outgroup as more aggressive than N.D.A. supporters do. Agreement with the statement that the typical outgroup member is more aggressive than the typical ingroup member did not differ between I.N.D.I.A. supporters (M = 6.01, SD = 2.45) and N.D.A. supporters (M = 5.95, SD = 2.35; d = 0.02, t(609) = 0.31, p = .760). Thus, here the asymmetry in outgroup perceptions of political violence support emerged even in the absence of asymmetries in affect or in general beliefs about the outgroup's aggressiveness.

Discussion

We conducted four pre-registered studies (N=3,439) focused on U.S. partisans (Studies 1-3) and Indian partisans (Study 4). In Studies 1-3, we provide evidence that reported support for political violence is rare, and both Democrats and Republicans significantly overestimate the prevalence of reported political violence support. Critically, across three studies and several outcomes, we find that Democrats exhibit greater pessimism towards Republicans' reported support for political violence than vice versa. This asymmetry emerged consistently across different types of political violence (Study 1), across different measurement formats (Study 2), across multiple nationally representative samples collected over a year apart (Studies 2 and 3), and across both the United States and India (Studies 1-4).

What might drive this asymmetry? Study 3 offers experimental evidence that exposure to a single (fictional) violent outparty exemplar causally increases perceived outparty support for political violence. Moreover, exposing Republicans to a violent outparty exemplar increased their estimates to match Democrats' baseline perceptions in the control condition. Mediation analyses reveal that the effect of violent exemplars operated through increased cognitive availability of violent outparty members, which in turn elevated beliefs about outparty aggressiveness and support for violence. This suggests that a vivid and extreme example of a violent outparty member can make similar instances of violent outparty members more cognitively available, leading partisans to overgeneralize the prevalence of such support within the outgroup. Similarly, within the control condition, we find evidence that violent outparty exemplars were more cognitively available to Democrats than Republicans. These findings align with availability-based accounts of social judgment (46) (47) (48) and provide the first evidence, to our knowledge, identifying psychological processes underlying inflated political misperceptions.

We note that Democrats exposed to a violent exemplar also increased their estimates of outparty political violence support relative to control, indicating that the observed partisan asymmetry does not reflect a rigid baseline bias among Democrats. Both Democrats and Republicans responded to a salient violent exemplar. In light of past work showing that partisans are often exposed to information that reinforces negative stereotypes of the outgroup (https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/KMBLf with Democrats potentially encountering more portrayals of Republican aggression (28) particularly following January 6th (29https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/8a73I+9ptTB 30) , our findings suggest that the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry may reflect different informational environments (50) (51) (52).

We do not find evidence that exposure to a non-violent outparty exemplar affects perceived outparty support for political violence among either Democrats or Republicans. This pattern suggests that partisans are not simply considering any outparty exemplar and assessing that exemplar's likely attitudes toward violence. Rather, it seems partisans specifically attempt to retrieve or imagine a violent outparty exemplar and then infer broader support for political violence based on how readily that exemplar comes to mind. The ease of accessing such an example (i.e., its cognitive availability) appears to shape perceptions of how widespread violent attitudes are within the outgroup. Additionally, meta-perceptions were largely unaffected by the manipulation, suggesting that beliefs about how one's own group is viewed by the outparty may be less malleable to isolated exemplars.

Study 4 indicates that this asymmetry is not unique to the United States. Among Indian partisans, supporters of the relatively left-leaning I.N.D.I.A. alliance were more pessimistic than N.D.A. alliance supporters about outgroup members' support for political violence.

Our findings extend prior research indicating that Americans often misperceive political outgroup members' attitudes (16). In addition to identifying cognitive availability of violent exemplars as a key mechanism, our work is the first to demonstrate a partisan asymmetry in outgroup perceptions of the prevalence of political violence support, and we find evidence of a similar asymmetry among Indian partisans. Notably, across all four studies, we do not observe a significant asymmetry in ingroup perceptions of support for political violence. We also do not observe a Democrat-Republican asymmetry in outgroup members' support for non-political crimes such as drug trafficking, and the asymmetry was significantly larger for political violence than for drug trafficking in Studies 2 and 3. This suggests that, among U.S. partisans, Democrats' heightened pessimism is specific to perceptions of reported political violence support among outgroup members. Research on partisan misperceptions indicates that such specificity may reflect the perceived danger of political violence relative to other issues, as individuals often perceive greater partisan differences among issues they consider important (53, 54).

Beyond cognitive availability, other factors may partially contribute to the Democrat-Republican asymmetry in outgroup perceptions of political violence support. Democrats reported more negative affect toward Republicans and more negative affective meta-perceptions. Thus, Democrats' pessimism toward Republicans' political violence support may partially reflect highly negative outgroup attitudes. This is consistent with our finding that Democrats also believed that Republicans viewed them as more likely to report supporting political violence than vice versa. However, affective differences do not appear to be strictly necessary for the asymmetry to emerge: in Study 4, I.N.D.I.A. supporters were more pessimistic than N.D.A. supporters about outgroup members' support for political violence even though the two groups did not differ in outgroup affect or affective meta-perceptions. Likewise, I.N.D.I.A. supporters held more pessimistic meta-perceptions of drug trafficking support despite no asymmetry in outgroup predictions for that crime, suggesting that more pessimistic meta-perceptions need not accompany more pessimistic outgroup perceptions. Future research should explore the extent to which these variables are causally linked.

Additionally, Democrats perceived the most extreme Republicans as more supportive of political violence than vice versa (Studies 2 and 3), and I.N.D.I.A. supporters showed the same pattern for the most extreme N.D.A. supporters (Study 4). Democrats may generalize from the actions or rhetoric of a salient subset of Republicans who seemingly endorse political violence (34) https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/vfyZu which increases Democrats' overall outgroup misperceptions about the pervasiveness of political violence support. Importantly, we note that these asymmetries may also reflect actual differences in political violence support among extreme Republicans and Democrats rather than biased intergroup processes on behalf of the average Democrat. Past research suggests that a subset of Republicans -namely Trump supporters who deny the validity of the 2020 electionare significantly more likely than other groups to support political violence (34). While prior work has not found partisan asymmetries in perceived outgroup violence support (16, 39), the continued visibility of these subgroups and of Donald Trump in recent public discourse may render extreme Republican exemplars more cognitively accessible to Democrats. This heightened salience could help explain the asymmetry observed in our studies. Nevertheless, given the low levels of political violence support observed among both U.S. parties, such perceptions of widespread self-reported support for political violence among outgroup members are likely misrepresentative of reality. However, we do not find evidence that the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry simply captures participants' exaggerating their stated perceptions, as providing financial incentives for accuracy did not significantly affect Democrats' or Republicans' outgroup predictions. This suggests that the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetries reflect genuine differences in outgroup perception.

Our findings are subject to several limitations. Here, we have focused on an online sample of self-identified Democrats and Republicans (Studies 1-3) and I.N.D.I.A. and N.D.A. alliance supporters (Study 4). Although Studies 2 and 3 use samples that are demographically representative of the U.S., online samples may differ from real-world populations. Similarly, although Study 4 uses a sample that is nationally representative with respect to politics, we relied on English-speaking participants who may differ from non-English speakers. Future research could explore the generalizability of this asymmetry among non-English speakers, as well as among other countries beyond the United States and India. Additionally, we rely on self-report data, which may be subject to social desirability bias, especially given the sensitivity of political violence support. Future research could, therefore, incorporate implicit measures and behavioral indicators to corroborate self-reported attitudes. Finally, partisans' tendency to overestimate the proportion of others, even inparty members, who support political violence may partially reflect general numeracy biases in cognition (55).

Taken together, these findings identify a consistent partisan asymmetry: Democrats perceive Republicans as more supportive of political violence than vice versa. This asymmetry holds across various forms of violence (Study 1) and measurement formats (Study 2), and is accompanied by Democrats expressing greater concern about outgroup extremists, more negative affect and meta-perceptions, and stronger beliefs in Republican aggressiveness (Studies 1-3). A similar asymmetry emerged among Indian partisans (Study 4), as I.N.D.I.A. supporters were more pessimistic than N.D.A. supporters about outgroup members. Study 3 identifies a causal mechanism underlying such partisan misperceptions. Exposure to a single violent outparty exemplar increased perceived outparty support for violence via heightened cognitive availability and, in turn, aggressiveness perceptions. This exposure eliminated the partisan gap by raising Republicans' estimates to match Democrats', suggesting that asymmetric exposure to violent outparty exemplars may help sustain real-world misperception gaps.

More broadly, these findings underscore the importance of tailoring interventions to different populations. Interventions aimed at correcting inflated beliefs about widespread outparty support for political violence may be especially impactful among Democrats and I.N.D.I.A. alliance supporters, whereas approaches targeting Republicans and N.D.A. alliance supporters may need to address other dimensions of partisan conflict. At the same time, our results highlight the risks of interventions or public discourse that emphasize extreme outparty actors: even a single salient exemplar was sufficient to elevate perceived outparty support for violence and erase baseline partisan differences. Thus, efforts to reduce misperceptions may be undermined by media environments, political rhetoric, or communication strategies that foreground extreme cases, inadvertently amplifying perceived threat. Promoting accurate beliefs about the true prevalence of political violence support while avoiding disproportionate focus on rare but dramatic instances may therefore be critical to reducing partisan fear and fostering a healthier democratic environment.

Methods

Ethics Statement and Reproducibility

All participants provided informed consent and received compensation for participation. All studies were approved by the Harvard University IRB. Pre-registrations are available at https://researchbox.org/4077&PEER_REVIEW_passcode=VXOCYQ (Studies 1, 2, and 4) and https://osf.io/muq59/overview?view_only=7093bebefbb34b5bb78b4d10e17d18df (Study 3). Materials, anonymized data, analysis code are available at https://osf.io/9tafn/?view_only=e4adb7c08b5a4ec28cc1847da6a4d725.

Study 1

All participants in Study 1 (N = 426) were recruited from Prolific on 07/18/2024. As preregistered (https://researchbox.org/4077&PEER_REVIEW_passcode=VXOCYQ), we excluded 10 participants who did not identify as either "Republican" or "Democrat" and 8 participants who failed an attention check. All remaining participants were included in the analyses (N = 408; 207 Democrats, 201 Republicans; 203 female; Mage = 38.6, SDage = 13.3).

To measure support for political violence, participants read each of the following vignettes, adapted from prior literature (https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/nQd9U and were asked: "Do you support or oppose [name's] actions?" Responses included "Support," "Neither support nor oppose," and "Oppose."

Arson: "[name] was convicted of arson. He was arrested by police after starting a fire at the local [outgroup] Party's headquarters. [name] targeted the headquarters because he believed that the [outgroup] Party is harmful to the nation's future." Assault with a deadly weapon: "[name] was convicted of assault with a deadly weapon. He was arrested by police after driving his car into a crowd of [outgroup] protesters. Although no one was killed, several individuals were seriously injured and one spent a month in the hospital. [name] targeted the victims because he believed that the [outgroup] Party is harmful to the nation's future." Murder: "[name] was convicted of murder. He was arrested by police after stabbing a prominent [outgroup] to death. [name] targeted the victim because he believed that the [outgroup] Party is harmful to the nation's future."

To measure perceptions of their outgroup/ingroup, participants were instructed, "Please indicate what percentage of [outgroup/ingroup] you believe will support [name's] actions. (Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)."

To measure meta-perceptions, participants were told, "We are asking [outgroup] to predict what percentage of [ingroup] will support [name's] actions. What do you think the average [outgroup]'s prediction will be? (Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)" To minimize potential confusion, participants received the following example: "For example, if you think that the average [outgroup] will predict that half of all [ingroup] would support [name's] actions, you would enter "50"."

To measure concern about outgroup/ingroup extremists, participants were asked to "Please take a moment to think about [outgroup] who support or are willing to engage in politically-motivated violence like the actions you just read. On a scale from 1 to 9, how much of a threat do you think these [outgroup/ingroup] pose to each of the following?" Participants responded using a 9-point scale ranging from "Not a threat at all" to "Extreme threat" for each of the following outcomes: Public Safety, Future Election Security, US Democracy, and America.

As an additional measure of concern, participants were asked, "On a scale from 1 to 9, how important do you think it is to protect against [outgroup/ingroup] who support or are willing to engage in politically-motivated violence?" Participants responded using a 9point scale ranging from "Not at all important" to "Extremely important."

To measure concern about civil war, participants were asked, "Are you concerned about the possibility of a civil war occurring in the United States?" Participants responded with a dichotomous "Yes" or "No."

To measure outgroup/ingroup perceptions about civil war concern, participants were asked to "Please indicate what percentage of [outgroup/ingroup] you believe are concerned about the possibility of civil war in the United States. (Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)."

Finally, as an attention check, participants were asked, "What was NOT covered in this study?" with the following randomly-ordered response options: Murder, Setting Fire, Driving a car into a crowd, Crashing a plane. Participants who did not select "Crashing a plane" were excluded from all analyses.

Study 2

Study 2 used a large representative sample (N = 1,589) recruited from Prolific during 08/22/2024 -08/26/2024. As pre-registered (https://researchbox.org/4077&PEER_REVIEW_passcode=VXOCYQ), we excluded 674 participants who did not identify as either "Republican" or "Democrat" and 8 participants who failed an attention check. We also excluded 1 participant whose responses included impossible values (e.g., predicting that 500% of outgroup members support drug trafficking). All remaining participants were included in the analyses (N = 906; 494 Democrats, 412 Republicans; 450 female; Mage = 46.9, SDage = 16.1).

As noted above, given the consistency of responses across all three measures in Study 1, in Study 2, we measured support for political violence using only the murder vignette. We also used the following vignette to explore misperceptions for a non-politicallymotivated, non-violent crime (drug trafficking): Drug Trafficking: "[name] was convicted of drug trafficking. He was arrested by police after transporting large quantities of heroin into local neighborhoods.

[name] targeted these areas because he believed that the demand for drugs would ensure him massive personal financial profits, regardless of the drugs' harmfulness." Participants' own support and ingroup, outgroup, and meta-perceptions were measured using identical procedures to Study 1. However, in Study 2, we randomly assigned half of our participants to receive financial incentives for accuracy (40). Participants assigned to receive accuracy incentives read the following instructions prior to making predictions about the outgroup: "You will earn a 50 cent bonus ($0.50) if your predictions are, on average, within 5 percentage points of the true value."

To measure concern about outgroup/ingroup extremists, participants were asked to "Please take a moment to think about [outgroup] who support or are willing to engage in politically-motivated violence like stabbing a prominent political figure to death." Otherwise, the procedures used to measure concern were identical to Study 1. Perceived importance of protecting against extremists and civil war concern were also measured using the same procedures as Study 1.

In Study 2, we added measures of perceived support for political violence among outgroup and ingroup leaders (e.g., elected officials), as well as among the most extreme outgroup and ingroup members.

To measure perceptions of outgroup and ingroup leaders, participants were instructed, "We are also interested in how you think leaders of the [outgroup/ingroup] Party (e.g., elected officials) would respond to similar questions. Please indicate what percentage of [outgroup/ingroup] leaders you believe will support [name's] actions. (Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)." To measure perceptions of the most extreme outgroup and ingroup members, participants were instructed, "Now, imagine a group of the most extreme [outparty/inparty] supporters. Please indicate what percentage of the most extreme [outgroup/ingroup] supporters you believe will support [name's] actions. (Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)."

We also assessed participants' perceptions of whether typical outgroup members are more aggressive than typical ingroup members using the following: "To what extent do you agree or disagree with the statement: The typical [outgroup] is more aggressive than the typical [ingroup]. "1" means "Strongly disagree" and "9" means "Strongly agree."

We also included an alternative measure of support for political violence used in previous studies (16, 41). Specifically, we ask (1) how much participants feel it is justified for [ingroup] to use violence in advancing their political goals these days, and (2) how much participants feel it is justified for [ingroup] to use violence if the [outgroup] Party wins the next presidential election. Responses for both items range from 0 ("Never") to 100 ("Always") (16). Participants then predicted the average ingroup and outgroup members' responses. Given ongoing debates regarding whether measures that contain ambiguous definitions of violence can meaningfully capture support for political violence (15), we randomly assigned half of our participants-stratified by political party-to respond to these alternative measures before the vignette-based measure.

We also measured ingroup, outgroup, and meta-perceptions of affect using standard feeling thermometers (42, 43). See SI for additional details.

Finally, as an attention check, participants were asked, "What was NOT covered in this study?" with the following randomly-ordered response options: Murder, Selling drugs, Civil war, and Crashing a plane. Participants who did not select "Crashing a plane" were excluded from all analyses.

Study 3

We recruited a large representative sample (N = 1,556) from Prolific during 10/23/2025 -10/27/2025. As pre-registered (https://osf.io/muq59/overview?view_only=7093bebefbb34b5bb78b4d10e17d18df), we excluded 37 participants who did not identify as either "Republican" or "Democrat" and 14 participants who failed an attention check. All remaining participants were included in the analyses (N = 1,505; 753 Democrats, 752 Republicans; 749 female; Mage = 45.7, SDage = 14.5).

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: exposure to a violent outparty exemplar, exposure to a non-violent outparty exemplar, or a pure control (no exemplar). In the two exemplar conditions, participants read a short description of an outparty member named "Bob" accompanied by a simple cartoon image. In the violent exemplar condition, Bob was described as follows: "Bob is a [Democrat/Republican] and an active member of radical political groups.

He feels constant anger about politics and believes that confrontation is necessary to defend his values. Bob often attends heated political rallies where fights break out, and he has engaged in violent behavior during these events. People describe him as intense, confrontational, quick-tempered, and driven by outrage."

In the non-violent exemplar condition, Bob was described as follows: "Bob is a [Democrat/Republican] and [works as a high school teacher/owns a family farm].

He loves spending time with his wife and kids, often coaching his son's soccer team on weekends. He believes strongly in promoting fairness and social responsibility, but he is careful to respect rules and order. Bob is calm, dependable, and has never harmed anyone. He's known in his community as someone who can always be trusted to do the right thing." Participants in either exemplar condition then rated how "typical" Bob was of the outparty (1-9 scale, "Not at all typical" to "Very typical").

We assessed three preregistered mechanisms. Cognitive availability of violent outparty members was measured by participants' level of agreement or disagreement with the statement, "It is easy for me to think of violent [Democrats/Republicans]" (1-9 scale, "Strongly disagree" to "Strongly agree"). Associative strength between violence and the outparty was measured by participants' level of agreement or disagreement with the statement, "When I think of [Democrats/Republicans], violent people come to mind" (1-9 scale, "Strongly disagree" to "Strongly agree"). Generalized beliefs about outparty aggressiveness were then measured as in Study 2.

As in Study 2, we used the murder vignette and, to assess misperceptions for nonpolitically-motivated, non-violent crime, the drug trafficking vignette.

Participants' own support and ingroup, outgroup, and meta-perceptions were measured using identical procedures to Study 1. Perceived support among outgroup and ingroup leaders, as well as the most extreme outgroup and ingroup members, were measured using identical procedures to Study 2. We also measured ingrouphttps://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/WkVXi+6Erub outgroup, and metaperceptions of affect using standard feeling thermometers (42, 43) , and we measured participants' own concern about a potential civil war using identical procedures to Studies 1 and 2. Finally, we use the same attention check as in Study 2.

Study 4

We recruited a large sample of Indian participants (N = 2,732) from Cint during 07/30/2026 -08/03/2026. As described below, we excluded participants in order to obtain a sample of English-speaking Indian participants who supported one of India's two major political alliances: the National Democratic Alliance (N.D.A.), a coalition led by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance (I.N.D.I.A.), an opposition coalition primarily led by the Indian National Congress (INC).

We recruited a politically representative sample using quotas based on participants' selfreported party affiliation (BJP, INC, CPI, AAP, BSP, NPP, or another party). As preregistered (https://researchbox.org/4077&PEER_REVIEW_passcode=VXOCYQ), we excluded participants who did not identify as supporters of either the N.D.A. alliance or the I.N.D.I.A. alliance (697 participants), who failed either of two Englishcomprehension items (1,327 participants), or who failed an attention check (88 participants). All remaining participants were included in the analyses (N = 620; 319 I.N.D.I.A. alliance supporters, 301 N.D.A. alliance supporters; 195 female; Mage = 30.4, SDage = 11.1).

Participants first reported which political party they support (BJP, INC, CPI, AAP, BSP, NPP, a different party, or none of the above), whether they consider themselves supporters of the N.D.A. alliance, the I.N.D.I.A. alliance, or neither, and their ideology ("In politics people sometimes talk of 'left' and 'right'. Where would you place yourself on this scale?" ;0 = left,10 = right). Participants who identified with either alliance were then assigned the other alliance as their outgroup. Because the survey was administered in English, participants also completed two English-comprehension items (a short reading-comprehension question and a sentence-completion item).

As in Studies 2 and 3, we used the murder vignette and, to assess misperceptions for nonpolitically-motivated, non-violent crime, the drug trafficking vignette. The murder vignette was adapted to the Indian context as follows:

Murder: "[name] was convicted of murder. He was arrested by police after stabbing a prominent [outgroup] member to death. [name] targeted the victim because he believed that the [outgroup] is harmful to the nation's future." where [outgroup] was either "N.D.A. alliance" or "I.N.D.I.A. alliance." The drug trafficking vignette was identical to that used in Study 2.

Participants' own support and ingroup, outgroup, and meta-perceptions were measured using procedures from Study 1, where [outgroup] was either "N.D.A. alliance" or "I.N.D.I.A. alliance." For example, to measure perceptions of their outgroup/ingroup, participants were instructed, "Please indicate what percentage of people who support the [outgroup/ingroup] you believe will support [name]'s actions. (Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)."

To measure concern about outgroup/ingroup extremists, participants were asked to "Please take a moment to think about [outgroup] supporters who support or are willing to engage in politically-motivated violence like stabbing a prominent political figure to death." Participants then rated how much of a threat these supporters pose to Public Safety, Future Election Security, India's Democracy, and India on a 9-point scale, and rated the importance of protecting against them, using the same procedures as Study 2. Concern about civil war and perceptions of outgroup/ingroup civil war concern were measured using the same procedures as Studies 1 and 2, with reference to the possibility of a civil war occurring in India.

As in Studies 2 and 3, we measured perceived support for political violence among outgroup and ingroup leaders (e.g., elected officials), as well as among the most extreme outgroup and ingroup supporters, using identical procedures to Study 2, and we assessed perceptions of whether typical outgroup members are more aggressive than typical ingroup members ("The typical [outgroup] supporter is more aggressive than the typical [ingroup] supporter"; 1-9 scale). We also measured ingroup, outgroup, and metaperceptions of affect using standard feeling thermometers (42, 43).

Finally, as an attention check, participants were asked, "What was NOT covered in this study?" with the following randomly-ordered response options: Murder, Selling drugs, Civil war, and Crashing a plane. Participants who did not select "Crashing a plane" were excluded from all analyses.
